title: Sugar in the iron bowl
hookLine: the Guru stirs water with a double-edged blade while reciting, and tradition says Mata Jito added sugar crystals

lines: AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.
cards: Vaisakhi, 1699. The five beloved stand beside the Guru, the crowd watching. He calls for an iron bowl and clean water.
He doesn't just pour it. He kneels, takes up a khanda, a double-edged sword, and stirs the water with the blade, round and round, while reciting hymns. It takes a long time.
A baby at a font, someone stepping down into a river: water is one way people say something new begins here. And then, tradition says, someone stepped forward and added one more thing.

teach.b: Amrit means the nectar of immortality, literally not-death. You met it inside the name Amritsar, the pool of nectar, on day fifty-five.
On Vaisakhi, 1699, amrit took on a new meaning: the sweetened water of Sikh initiation.

teach.h: THE KHANDA STIRS, HYMNS ARE SUNG.
teach.b: As Sikh tradition tells it: clean water in an iron bowl, the Guru stirring it with the khanda while reciting five hymns, among them the Japji of Guru Nanak and the Anand, the song of bliss you met on day fifty-three.
The bowl is iron, and the blade is steel: strength, courage, readiness. Then the sweetness.

Tradition says the Guru's wife, Mata Jito, came with sugar puffs, patashe, and dropped them into the water. Some accounts name Mata Sahib Kaur instead; the sources differ, and Sikhs tell it both ways.
Either way, the meaning Sikhs draw from it is the same. The blade alone would make the water hard. The sugar alone would make it soft.
Together, strength and sweetness. The Khalsa was to be brave, and also gentle. Firm, and kind.
Then the Guru gave the amrit to the five, sprinkling it on their eyes and hair and giving it to them to drink, all from the same bowl, men of different castes drinking together.
That was the point too. The practice continues today as amrit sanchar: five initiated Sikhs, standing as the Panj Pyare, prepare the amrit the same way.

how: Sikhs who choose to be initiated take amrit in a ceremony called amrit sanchar, where five initiated Sikhs prepare sweetened water in an iron bowl, stirring it with a khanda while reciting five banis.

o: a healing oil rubbed on the forehead at birth
a morning hymn sung to start the Sikh day
sweet water stirred with a blade at initiation

games.q: you're preparing the water of initiation. it's been stirred with a double-edged blade. what do you add?
games.why: tradition says sugar puffs were added: strength from the blade, sweetness from the sugar, together.

practice: If you can, pour a glass of water, add a little sugar, honey or a slice of fruit, and stir it slowly, watching it dissolve; if not, just picture it.
As you stir, think of one place in your life where you've been all strength and no sweetness, or all sweetness and no strength. Then drink slowly, and let the two come together.

wordCard.voice: Amrit. The nectar of immortality; for Sikhs, the sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, given at initiation.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Sanskrit amṛta: not-death, the nectar of immortality.

carryVoice: Your line: strength and sweetness. A blade and a handful of sugar, in one bowl. Day eighty-six.
